title: API 653 Training in Baton Rouge: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced online API 653 exam prep for Baton Rouge tank inspectors at refinery tank fields, Port Allen terminals and chemical storage, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 653 Training in Baton Rouge: Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Refinery Tank Fields, River Terminals and Chemical Storage
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors around Baton Rouge

Aboveground storage tanks are everywhere on this stretch of the Mississippi: crude, intermediate and product tanks in the refinery tank fields, heated fuel oil and asphalt tanks at river terminals, chemical tanks at the plants downstream and liquid bulk storage served by ships and barges at the port. API 653 certification is the credential that inspection departments, terminal operators and their contractors look for when someone has to judge whether a tank's shell, floor and roof are fit to stay in service. This page is for the tank inspectors, floor-scan technicians, tank construction crews and terminal staff in and around Baton Rouge who are preparing for that exam.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Baton Rouge. The API 653 course runs self-paced online, with an instructor answering questions as you study, so it fits around terminal shifts and refinery rosters. The American Petroleum Institute sets eligibility under Annex D of API 653, administers the exam at Prometric test centres and issues the certification; the course prepares you for that exam and confers no certification of its own.

Who stores what along the river at Baton Rouge

EIA's refinery capacity survey for 2026 lists ExxonMobil's Baton Rouge refinery at 523,500 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation and Placid's Port Allen refinery at 75,000. Refineries of that size hold crude, intermediate and finished product in their own tank fields, so a good share of the area's API 653 work sits inside the two refinery fences. The Port of Greater Baton Rouge adds commercial storage. Its own pages list these liquid bulk terminals:

Terminal (port listing)Storage stated by the portProducts and services
Center Point Terminal Company, a subsidiary of Apex Oil Company1,215,000 barrelsNo. 2 through No. 6 fuel oils, asphalt and carbon black; dockside steam boilers for heating products; ship, barge, rail and truck access
BWC Terminals22 million gallonsIndustrial grade molasses and specialty chemicals; deepwater, barge, rail and truck access with a rail transfer terminal
John W. Stone Oil Distributornot stated on the port pageListed among the port's liquid bulk terminals

The port's directory of liquid cargo facilities also names Genesis Energy and LBC Baton Rouge. LBC Tank Terminals, whose US storage terminals include Baton Rouge, Houston and Freeport, has been owned by the Japanese shipping group Mitsui O.S.K. Lines since the acquisition completed in mid-2025. Downstream, the chemical plants at Plaquemine and Geismar keep their own feed and product tank fields, and the nitrogen complex at Donaldsonville stores ammonia and fertilizer products, though not all of that storage falls under API 653, as the next section explains.

Which tanks are API 653 tanks, and which belong to other codes

API 653 was written for in-service atmospheric steel tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C, and owners apply it to other steel tanks built to a tank specification. Around Baton Rouge that leaves several kinds of storage that need care before you count them as API 653 experience or answer an exam question about them:

  • Heated fuel oil and asphalt tanks. Still API 653 tanks, but often insulated, fitted with heating coils, and sometimes designed under API 650's annex for elevated-temperature service, which changes the allowable stress basis and adds corrosion under insulation on the shell and roof.
  • Refrigerated ammonia and other low-temperature storage. Built to low-pressure standards such as API 620 and API 625; API 653's shell and floor rules were not written for them.
  • Pressurised spheres and bullets. Pressure vessels, inspected under API 510, not tanks under API 653.
  • Small shop-built tanks. EPA notes that STI SP001 focuses mainly on welded shop-fabricated and small field-erected tanks, while API 653 is typically used for field-erected tanks.
  • Stainless, alloy and lined chemical tanks. The scope statement, the construction annex on the nameplate and the owner's procedure all matter more than usual, and product-specific damage needs research before entry.

The rules that put an inspector on a Baton Rouge tank

Three sets of federal rules bring API 653 inspectors to local tanks.

  • Spill prevention (SPCC). 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6) tells oil facilities to test or inspect each aboveground container for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made. EPA's integrity testing factsheet leaves the choice of industry standard to the owner or operator, describes API 653 as the standard typically used for field-erected tanks and says formal API 653 inspections are conducted by an API 653 certified inspector, while frequent external visual checks can be done by trained facility staff.
  • Process safety and risk management. Storage tanks in a covered process fall under the mechanical integrity paragraph of OSHA's process safety management standard, and EPA's 40 CFR 68.73 lists pressure vessels and storage tanks first among the equipment its inspection and testing rules apply to.
  • Pipeline breakout tanks. Under 49 CFR 195.432 each in-service breakout tank gets a routine inspection at least once each calendar year, at intervals not exceeding 15 months, and atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks are inspected to API 653, excluding its risk-based alternative for setting the internal interval. Louisiana's administrative code carries a matching section that cites 49 CFR 195.432. PHMSA proposed changes in 2026; until a final rule is published, the current text applies.

The exam tests API 653 and its referenced documents, not these regulations, but knowing why a tank is inspected tells you which interval rules you will actually use on the job. The SPCC inspector guide and the API 653 interval guide go further.

Tank floors on wet, low-lying ground

Baton Rouge averages close to 62 inches of precipitation a year on NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals, and the river parishes are flat delta country. Water that collects at the chime, foundations that hold moisture and pads that settle unevenly are the background to many floor and shell findings. For an API 653 candidate the local lesson is that the soil side of the floor is often the one that decides the next interval.

  • Soil-side corrosion and cathodic protection. API RP 651 covers cathodic protection of tank bottoms, and the floor rules in API 653 treat the underside corrosion rate as its own term, so a floor scan without the CP history tells only half the story.
  • Internal linings. API RP 652 covers bottom linings, and a sound lining changes how the product-side rate is treated in the same calculation.
  • Release prevention barriers. Whether a tank has a means of detecting and containing a bottom leak changes the minimum floor thickness the code accepts; the release prevention barrier guide explains the difference.
  • Settlement. Annex B of API 653 sets out how settlement is measured and evaluated, and soft ground makes those surveys a routine part of local tank work; see the settlement guide.

The tank floor remaining thickness guide and the API 653 course page work the floor formula with numbers.

Worked example: averaging a corroded area on a terminal tank shell

Shell corrosion on an old tank is rarely uniform, and API 653 does not make the inspector reject a course because of its single thinnest reading. For a corroded area it sets a critical length over which hoop stress is assumed to average out: L = 3.7 × √(D × t2), but not more than 40 in., where D is the tank diameter in feet, t2 is the least thickness in the area in inches, excluding widely scattered pits, and L comes out in inches. The inspector then takes at least five equally spaced readings along the most affected vertical plane over that length and averages them to get t1.

Take a hypothetical 150 ft diameter heated fuel oil tank whose first course has a minimum required thickness tmin of 0.400 in., and a corroded patch with a least reading t2 of 0.290 in.

  • L = 3.7 × √(150 × 0.290) = 3.7 × √43.5 = 3.7 × 6.595 = 24.4 in.
  • Readings along the worst vertical line over 24.4 in. average t1 = 0.415 in., which meets tmin of 0.400 in.
  • The second test is t2 against 60 percent of tmin: 0.6 × 0.400 = 0.240 in., and 0.290 in. passes.
  • Both results must still hold after the corrosion expected before the next inspection, which is the question that usually follows.

Change the tank and the length changes. A 30 ft chemical tank with t2 of 0.150 in. gives L = 3.7 × √4.5 = 7.8 in. A 260 ft crude tank with t2 of 0.850 in. gives 3.7 × √221 = 55.0 in., so the 40 in. cap governs. Widely scattered pits are handled separately: API 653 lets them be ignored when no pit leaves less than half the minimum acceptable shell thickness, excluding corrosion allowance, and the sum of their dimensions along any vertical line is no more than 2 in. in an 8 in. length. Exam questions often mix the two rules, so read whether the figures describe an area or scattered pits before you reach for a formula.

Routes into API 653 for Baton Rouge tank people

Annex D of API 653 sets the experience requirement, counting work within the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. With a bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology, one year supervising or performing tank inspection activities; with a two-year degree or certificate, two years in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of aboveground storage tanks, one of them in inspection; with a high school diploma, three years on the same basis; and with no formal education, five or more. Technical military service can stand in for the degree routes.

  • Floor-scan and UT technicians. MFL floor scanning, shell thickness surveys and weld examination for a terminal or refinery inspection programme are performing inspection. Baton Rouge Community College's workforce NDT programme and Atlantis's ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Baton Rouge are two ways into that work.
  • Tank construction and repair crews. Building and repairing tanks counts toward the total, and welding inspection is a common step between the two; see AWS CWI exam prep in Baton Rouge.
  • Terminal operators. Operating years count, but the inspection year has to come from an inspection role, such as a terminal's integrity or tank inspection group.
  • Engineers. A graduate engineer in a refinery or terminal integrity group can qualify after a year of genuine inspection work.

API verifies the experience you document. The API 653 certification page sets out the rules in full.

Studying API 653 around terminal and refinery schedules

Terminal work follows ship and barge movements and refinery tank work follows the turnaround and cleaning plan, so few candidates can promise the same study hours every week. The self-paced format absorbs that: work through API 653 and API 650 in the slack weeks, and keep short sessions on the closed-book rules going when a tank is out of service and reports are due. When an API 650 paragraph and an API 653 rule seem to conflict, the instructor's answer shows which document governs and where.

Exam day has 170 questions, 140 scored, split 110 closed-book and 60 open-book over 7.5 hours. The open-book half puts API 653, API 650 and the other publications on your window's effectivity sheet in front of you as PDFs, typically including RP 575, RP 651, RP 652, RP 571, RP 577 and the ASME Section V and IX references; check the sheet for your window. Prometric lists test centres in and around Baton Rouge, and the exam schedule gives the windows and deadlines.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Baton Rouge terminal or refinery

Terminal operators, refinery inspection groups and tank contractors can enrol several people under one quote; fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually with their own experience record. A sponsor gets the most from a group when each candidate is attached to real tank work while studying, a floor scan, a shell survey or an out-of-service inspection report, so that the code reading and the field work line up.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in person in Baton Rouge?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Baton Rouge. The API 653 course is self-paced online with instructor Q&A, so terminal and refinery staff study on their own schedule. The exam is taken in person at a Prometric test centre after API accepts your application, and API issues the certification to those who pass.

faq.q: Do refrigerated ammonia tanks count toward API 653 experience?
faq.a: Be careful. Refrigerated and low-pressure tanks are built to standards such as API 620 and API 625, and API 653's rules were written for atmospheric tanks built to API 650 and its predecessors. Inspection work on them may still be relevant experience, but API decides; describe the tanks and your role exactly on the application rather than calling them API 653 tanks.

faq.q: Does SPCC mean a Port Allen terminal needs an API 653 certified inspector?
faq.a: Often, for field-erected tanks. The SPCC rule requires integrity testing to an industry standard chosen by the owner or operator, and EPA's factsheet says formal inspections under API 653 are carried out by an API 653 certified inspector. Shop-built tanks may follow STI SP001 instead, and routine external checks can be done by trained facility staff.

faq.q: Are heated asphalt and fuel oil tanks inspected under API 653?
faq.a: Yes, if they are atmospheric steel tanks built to API 650 or a similar specification. Heating adds its own concerns: insulation that hides shell corrosion, heating coils inside the tank and, for tanks designed for elevated temperature, a different allowable stress basis. Expect exam questions to test whether you notice the design temperature.

faq.q: How often does a pipeline breakout tank in Louisiana need inspecting?
faq.a: Under 49 CFR 195.432, repeated in Louisiana's administrative code, each in-service breakout tank gets a routine inspection at least once each calendar year at intervals not exceeding 15 months, and atmospheric steel breakout tanks are inspected to API 653 without its risk-based internal interval option. A 2026 PHMSA proposal would change this; check whether it has become final.

faq.q: Do I need to study API 650 as well as API 653?
faq.a: Yes. API 650 is normally on the effectivity sheet for API 653 because repairs, alterations and reconstruction refer back to it for welding, examination and design. The exam does not test the whole of API 650, so use the Body of Knowledge to see which parts matter for your window.

faq.q: Where do Baton Rouge candidates sit the API 653 exam?
faq.a: At a Prometric test centre. Prometric lists centres in and around Baton Rouge, and you choose one once API has approved your application for an exam window. The exam is computer-based and in person; no books or papers are allowed, and the code PDFs are provided on screen for the open-book half.
